#10469. How to Add AI Content Detection to Your Node.js App

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sooner or later someone on your team asks it. Maybe it’s a product manager, maybe the head of content, maybe a teacher who’s just marked forty near-identical essays: can we tell when people are pasting in ChatGPT output?

The short answer is no, not with certainty. Anyone who promises you that is selling something.

But you can get a useful signal, and you can show it to the people who actually make the call: editors, teachers, moderators. In this tutorial you’ll build a small Express app that takes some text, sends it to an AI detector API, waits for the result, and highlights the sentences that look machine-written.

I’m using the Quetext AI Detector API here. It scores each sentence, not just the whole document, and you can try it without a subscription. Most detection APIs follow the same submit, poll, fetch pattern, though. If you switch providers later, you’ll rewrite one file.

Put the key in an environment variable. Don’t hard-code it, and don’t let it anywhere near the browser.

You’ll make three calls. Analysis takes a few seconds, so the API hands you a ticket and makes you come back for the result. Keep the Quetext API docs open in another tab while you follow along; they list every endpoint, field and error code.

Every request sends your key in an X-API-Key header. The minimum input is 50 words, which sounds annoying until you realise no detector can say anything useful about a two-line comment.

And remember this number: 10 requests every 5 seconds, per account. Progress checks count. It’ll come back to bite you in the production section if you ignore it.

Create quetext.js. I like keeping everything provider-specific in one file, so the rest of the app has no idea who’s doing the detecting.

Three decisions in there that are worth a sentence each:

The errors keep their HTTP status code. A 402 means you’ve run out of credit and a 429 means you’re polling too fast, and you’ll want to handle those differently from “something broke.”

It polls every 2.5 seconds because Quetext’s docs suggest 2 to 3. Polling faster won’t speed the report up. You’ll just burn through the rate limit.

And there’s a hard timeout. Leave it out and one stuck report can hang a request forever. That’s a miserable bug to track down at 11pm.

Next, server.js. It checks the input, runs the three calls, and gives the frontend a simple response that doesn’t mention Quetext anywhere.

Look at the mapping at the end. generated_prob becomes probability, and ai_score comes back as a string like "82.50", so it gets parsed into a number. It’s a small detail. But it means your frontend never learns which provider’s field names it’s dealing with, and that’s what makes swapping providers a one-file change.

Show someone “64% AI” and they’ll jump to a conclusion. Show them a paragraph with three sentences shaded pink and they’ll actually read it.

So the page shows every sentence, coloured by how likely it is to be AI-generated. Create public/index.html:

Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000. Try two samples: something you wrote yourself, then a raw chatbot answer on the same topic. Seeing which sentences light up teaches you more about how these detectors work than any diagram I could draw.

A quick security point. Those sentences came from your users, then went through an outside service. Treat them as untrusted. That’s why the code uses textContent and never innerHTML, as the OWASP XSS prevention cheat sheet recommends.

The demo keeps an HTTP request open while it polls. Fine on your laptop. Not fine with real traffic.

Submit the text, save the report id with a pending status, and respond straight away. A worker (BullMQ, a cron job, a serverless queue, whatever you already use) does the polling and updates the record once it’s done. The UI says “Checking…” until the result shows up.

Here’s how it goes wrong. It’s Monday morning, 20 editors open their review queues and click “Check” at roughly the same time. Each request polls on its own, and within a few seconds you’ve hit 429s across the board, because the 10-per-5-seconds limit covers your whole account, not each user.

Use one worker that loops through every pending report, with a short pause between calls. Problem solved.

You pay per word, so don’t check every blog comment. Article submissions, assignments and paid freelance work usually justify the cost. Cache results against a hash of the text too. Someone who submits the same draft three times shouldn’t cost you three times.

AI detection doesn’t catch copying. Someone can lift a 2019 blog post word for word and it’ll score 0% AI, because a human wrote it. Just not this human. If originality matters to your product, the same API has plagiarism endpoints that work exactly the same way. The API documentation covers both.

Developers skip this part. It’s also the part that ends up in angry support tickets.

In 2023, Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran essays written by non-native English speakers (all human, written for the TOEFL) through seven AI detectors. On average, the detectors labelled more than 61% of them as AI-generated. Simple vocabulary and textbook grammar read as “predictable,” and predictability is exactly what detectors look for.

Picture an international student getting an automatic zero because a script said so. You don’t want to be the person who built that.

Do that and the detector is a fast first pass that points people at what’s worth a closer look. Your humans still make the call.

You send text, the service checks how predictable each sentence would be to a language model, and you get back a probability that a machine wrote it. Most of these APIs are asynchronous. You submit, get a report ID, poll until it’s ready, then fetch the result. The better ones score individual sentences as well as the whole text, which makes building a sensible review screen much easier.

More than you’d think. Quetext’s API won’t accept fewer than 50 words, and in practice scores settle down once you’re past about 300. A product title or a one-line comment just doesn’t give a detector enough to go on. For short content, either group related pieces together or don’t bother checking it.

No. Detectors make mistakes, and research shows they flag non-native English writers far more often than native speakers. Use the score to decide what a human looks at first, not to block anything. Give reviewers the highlighted sentences, give users a way to explain themselves, and log what you decided. Your users get treated fairly and your support team avoids a pile of angry tickets.

Poll at the speed the provider recommends (every 2 to 3 seconds for Quetext), and remember that those polls count against your limit too. Once you’re in production, move checks into a background queue and let one worker poll every pending report, rather than having each user request poll by itself. When you do get a 429, wait a moment and retry.

No. If the browser calls the API directly, your key ends up in the frontend code where anyone can copy it and spend your credit. Keep the key in an environment variable on your server and send requests through your own endpoint, like the one in this tutorial. That also gives you somewhere to check input length, apply per-user limits and cache results before you pay for anything.

#10468. How Norway flipped Trump’s name-calling into destination marketing

After President Donald Trump called Norway a “shithouse country,” its tourism agency turned the insult into a marketing opportunity to promote its designer bathrooms.

Trump criticized Norway at a rally in Michigan on October 25 because he didn’t receive the Nobel Peace Prize, which is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee. Disparaging the Nordic nation with a term he’s previously used for Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia, and Yemen, Trump said he didn’t want immigrants from Norway. Now its tourism agency has turned the attack into a badge of honor with a website for the world’s best toilets that’s drawing eyes from across the globe.

While Visit Norway has had a web page about its public toilets for several years owing to their dramatic views and better than average design, the group changed the headline of the page to reference Trump’s comments and reshared it last week. It’s currently Visit Norway’s most popular page in most countries and has had 200,000 page views since Monday, while related social media posts have generated 5 million organic views so far, Visit Norway tells Fast Company.

The updated web page says “Norway makes shithouses great again!” and shows off some of the country’s most scene-stealing public accommodations across Norwegian Scenic Routes, a collection of some of the 18 prettiest drives in the country.

Among them are the Stegastein Lookout restroom, which looks out over a fjord, was designed by the architects Todd Saunders and Tommie Wilhelmsen, and won a Norwegian National Construction Prize. The restroom at Ureddplassen, a seaside memorial designed by Haugen/Zohar Architects that honors those killed on a Norwegian submarine by a German mine during World War II, is housed inside a wave-shaped building made from poured concrete with frosted glass windows, and it’s been called “the world’s most beautiful public loo.”

“Along the Norwegian Scenic Routes, architecture and design are used deliberately to enhance the experience of traveling through some of Norway’s most dramatic landscapes,” says Visit Norway’s head of consumer marketing, Anne-Signe Fagereng. “Leading architects have designed rest stops, viewpoints, and public toilets that fit into the landscape. Many have won international architecture awards, and several have become attractions in their own right. Travelers come to see them, photograph them and, yes, use them.”

A well-designed stop takes pressure off nature, makes remote areas accessible to everyone, and turns a necessary break into part of the experience, she says.

What Visit Norway’s selected restrooms have in common is thoughtful architecture and prime locations, like the rest area at Flesefossen waterfall or the restrooms at Skjervsfossen, which has glass floors and windows that look out over a river and was designed by the architectural firm Fortunen. The Oslo-based firm Snøhetta designed its service building at a hill called Kvalhausen as if it’s coming out of the hill.

Americans marvel at the cleanliness of bathrooms at truck stops like Buc-ee’s or Maverick, but in Norway, the best public restrooms show what’s possible when a government really invests in their services. Norwegian Scenic Routes is run by the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, or Statens Vegvesen.

Visit Norway says the updated site isn’t a political statement or broader criticism of anyone specifically—it’s just destination marketing. And it seems to be working. The tourism agency says it’s received many positive messages from Americans who say they want to visit. Now thanks to Trump’s comments, rest stops are on their to-do list.

#10466. Google stock drops amid AI fears; AI Mode has ‘lower monetization,’ getting more ads

Google is bringing ads to AI Mode globally as it admits that the new take on Search brings “lower monetization,” all while $GOOG stock is seeing a fairly major drop.

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call yesterday saw Google’s Philipp Schindler acknowledging that AI Mode, the company’s Gemini-powered new take on Search, has “lower monetization” compared to traditional Search. So the “strong growth” of AI Mode didn’t have as much of a positive impact on Google’s bottom line simply because the mode doesn’t generate as much revenue.

…It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we’re seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we’re now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries…

In a blog post the same day, Google announced that AI Mode would be getting ads in global markets. US users will also start to see “multiturn ads” in follow-up queries.

Our research shows that people are comfortable with ads in AI Mode and find them highly relevant. In fact, click-through rates are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.

Now we’re scaling ads in AI Mode in Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Singapore. In Q4 2026, we plan to expand to additional locales, including Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, $GOOG stock dipped by 27 points around the time of the earnings call and has continued to drop on October 29. It currently sits around $280, just a few points higher than a March 30 low of $273.14. The 12% drop reduces Google’s market cap by over $500 billion. NBC News points out that it is the second-biggest drop behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025.

The drop is not directly due to AI Mode itself, but is attributed to weaker-than-expected earnings in Q3. Ad revenue from Search still makes up roughly half of Google’s overall revenue.

Our Daniel Bader expands on this in the latest issue of Inbox, our twice-weekly free newsletter:

…But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

#10465. Bluesky was right all along and will accept your apology any time

Bluesky is a niche Twitter-clone frequently accused of being an echo chamber for progressives. After the blue tsunami of this week’s midterms, however, its inhabitants don’t seem to be echoing themselves so much as the vast majority of American voters.

The sheer scale of Democrats’ victory is staggering. They won control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, flipping Senate seats in seven states Trump carried in 2024—including Republican stronghold Texas, which now also has a Democratic governor and attorney general. All in all, this year’s midterms represent the biggest electoral shift in state-level politics to hit the U.S. in generations. They also represent a Texas-sized validation of the worldview Bluesky has become notorious for over the past two years.

Although it officially launched in the spring of 2023, Bluesky might as well have been born on election eve in 2024. That was the moment millions of disillusioned Twitter users decamped from a website owned by the largest single contributor to Trump’s reelection. Bluesky quickly became a haven for Twitter expats and grew at a frenetic pace. It went from 9 million users in September 2024 to 15 million by mid-November, eventually reaching its current 47 million.

Because many of Bluesky’s users arrived out of principled opposition to X, formerly Twitter, the two sites have arguably existed in opposition to each other. Both portray their counterpart as out of touch, with Bluesky alleging Elon Musk’s algorithm tweaks have skewed X’s political vortex too far to the right, and X suggesting Bluesky is a bubble of liberals who can tolerate anything except a difference in opinion.

The latter idea seemed to largely prevail. 

In 2025, Washington Post columnists, tech world figures like Mark Cuban, and myriad other pundits dismissed Bluesky as smug, self-righteous, and irrelevant. It was the fantasy sandbox where progressives went to play among themselves, protecting reality dwellers from having to hear their drivel. (“Like a containment dome over a nuclear reactor,” as the writer Josh Barro put it.)

So, how well did Bluesky’s users stay in touch with reality between elections, compared with X’s exponentially larger population? Consider the post-midterms perspective.

Rather than accept the narrative that 2024 represented a rejection of “wokeness” and a political realignment toward Trump, the manifestly trans-friendly Bluesky suggested the election was more a referendum on postpandemic inflation and global anti-incumbent bias. As an emboldened Trump then proceeded to antagonize U.S. citizens and the rest of the world, while making billions for himself in crypto, Bluesky meticulously chronicled the state of play. It became the premier destination for seeing radicalized older white ladies, abysmally attended pro-ICE rallies, and complaints about the lack of mainstream news coverage around massive No Kings protests. Any random day would find endless posts with evidence that, per the motto of the political philosopher and Bluesky power user Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò, “We are going to win.” 

Above all, Bluesky proved to be less a bubble than an expression of the multitude of ideological factions that had united under the umbrella of non-MAGAness . . . to argue with one another.

Meanwhile, X’s millions of liberal and progressive folks were often drowned out by an algorithm that seemed to favor right-wing voices and their preferred narratives. A bubble chart from Nate Silver, the political analyst, visually depicted the accounts with highest engagement rates back in April. Its many MAGA-red circles made it look like the blood-filled elevator from The Shining. As a May 2026 study from Northwestern University suggests, X’s algorithm rewards posts that provoke strong reactions, so the loudest and most emotionally satisfying political claims become disproportionately visible. That’s how we got viral fever dreams about James Talarico, the then-senatorial candidate, checking into a mental hospital, something that never in fact happened.

It should come as little surprise that many high-profile MAGA voices on X spent the days leading up to the election incorrectly predicting how it would turn out.

Who looks out of touch and stuck in an echo chamber now?

While X may have been more plugged into the political discourse online for the past two years, Bluesky now appears better attuned to what’s been happening on the ground. Its users were right about pretty much everything. 

They were right that anti-trans ads would have little or no impact on the 2026 election, and that their impact on the previous election had been vastly overstated.

They were right that Graham Platner wasn’t the only Democrat who could beat Susan Collins in Maine, and that Abdul El-Sayed’s association with a controversial Twitch streamer relatively few voters had even heard of was not as big a deal as X users seemed to think. 

And they were right that fleeing X’s algorithm helped them view the world with clear eyes.

If Bluesky is a bubble, then it is currently a champagne bubble awash in celebration.

The festivities will likely last only a matter of hours, though, until infighting explodes around just how the Democrats should spend their newfound political capital.

#10463. Google Home update should make Gemini stop saying ‘Sorry, I didn’t understand’ so much

Google’s latest Gemini for Home update targets a few issues, like one where speakers randomly blurt out “I didn’t understand” when no one asks.

The second October Gemini for Home update was released by Google today. It bundles a few fixes with a lengthy section in the changelog dedicated to the Google Home app.

I would probably tell Gemini, "Here, do you understand this?" as I threw it out the window

But there are six individual changes for Gemini within the Home app. One fix stands out the most, though. According to the update post, Google was aware that Home and Nest speakers/displays were facing a bug that would prompt them to say “Sorry, I didn’t understand” at random. That would happen unprompted, which is understandably a little unsettling. That strange bug should be fixed in this new update.

Further down, two fixes target Gemini’s ability to understand users on Google Home devices. For one, it would misunderstand requests to move music from one room to another. In other cases, it would incorrectly adjust sleep, media, or normal timers instead of the requested type. Both of those features will reportedly work as intended going forward.

The changelog includes a couple of other adjustments, which should make for an overall less stressful experience.

Updates should be live for users starting today, though it might take some time for them to roll out to everyone. Hopefully, Gemini will only let you know it doesn’t understand if it genuinely doesn’t understand.

#10462. Apple’s Music Hall signals a bigger strategic plan

Why would Apple launch a concert venue?

This is the question I’ve been asking myself since it inaugurated its Apple Music Hall, nestled underneath its U.K. headquarters at London’s Battersea Power Station, in late September. Not just any performance space, this intimate 600-person, 48-speaker hall features Apple’s Spatial Audio technology, which uses Dolby Atmos and dynamic head tracking to turn flat stereo sound into a three-dimensional, 360-degree experience.

To my eye, the Music Hall is not just another listening room. It’s the start of an elaborate world-building exercise for Apple Music, designed to engage a community of hardcore fans. In doing so, Apple is looking to increase streaming subscriptions, convert artists to recording on its technology, and eventually challenge everyone from Google Home to Sonos for ownership of our in-home sound delivery systems.

An uphill battle

In just eight years since entering the TV market, Apple has shifted from startup streamer to a television mecca, delivering hit after hit including Severance, Slow Horses, Silo, Pluribus, Ted Lasso, and now Widow’s Bay. Astounding.

Meanwhile, in music it’s played second fiddle to Spotify, which not only boasts three times as many subscribers, but is first with innovative ideas like its Year End Review and the exclusive content serious listeners crave most. The Music Hall is Apple turning up the volume.

The risks here are real. While global spend on IRL brand experiences grew 8.3% to $138.9 billion in 2025 and is projected to rise a further 10.3% in 2026, the highways to hell have far outstripped the stairways to heaven. Samsung 837, the company’s former experiential space in New York City’s Meatpacking District, succeeded in attracting mothers with young children looking for rainy day distractions but few potential customers. Many car companies—Lexus, Genesis, Cadillac—have tried their hand at luxury lounges, only to be reminded that consumers are looking to them for, well, cars.


Those that are true to their roots, however, are hitting all the right notes. A24, the film and TV production company, experienced a huge brand win with its acquisition last year of the historic Cherry Lane Theater in NYC’s West Village. This has been a launchpad for new and experimental content that in turn has led to greater visibility for the studio, deeper fan engagement, and a two-year brand partnership with Dior. Porsche’s Experience Centers delight driving enthusiasts and attract new customers with authentic racing outings.

In seemingly sparing no expense to create a world-class performance space, Apple is signaling to audiophiles everywhere that it is serious about building the world of Apple Music.

Building a successful brand world

Three essential elements go into building a successful brand world. The first is the Functional Offer, quite simply what the brand makes. For example, Volvo builds cars. The second is the Emotional Promise, which is how a brand is experienced emotionally. Through good Scandinavian design Volvo makes people feel great driving them. The third is the Cultural Quest. This is the way the brand engages with the world or a larger topic it constantly explores. For Volvo it is to have no one die in its vehicles. Ever.

All brands achieve the first; many achieve the second; very few achieve the third. The Music Hall gives Apple a route to achieving all three: not only producing and distributing music (offer), or making people feel good while listening (promise), but in our increasingly isolated, AI-fueled world, bringing music fans together around the highest quality, most authentic audio experiences, be they physical or digital (quest).

The key is cultivating a community engaging in meaningful participation around a brand world that is authentic to music.

The key question is, therefore, “How might Apple cultivate this passionate community of music fans?”

Lean into the community

Apple Music will need to do more than deliver music. It will need to become synonymous with the production and presentation of the world’s finest content. Opening with Elton John was a signal of intent.

Baby Keem, Skye Newman, Troye Sivan, Arlo Parks, Burna Boy, Chase & Status, Charli XCX—a real lineup to be sure. Now imagine that with its war chest, Apple starts attracting more prominent acts, and that music (sounding better recorded on Spatial Audio) is available only through a subscription on Apple Music.

The athletic wear brands like On and Bandit have been very successful with their run clubs. Might Apple establish its version? In partnership with Apple Pay and a major credit card company, early access to events is not hard to imagine. Nor are listening parties at the coolest venues for those who can’t attend events in person.

What’s at stake?

In its services division, Apple has shown with Pay and Health that it likes opportunities with huge addressable markets that plug in nicely to its hardware ecosystem. The global home audio hardware market, whose current players have set a fairly low bar, is valued at approximately $43.2 billion in 2026. If Apple can capture a good share of smart home audio and combine that with a greater share of the $54.54 billion global audio streaming market, the dollars become very real.

By striking the right chord between premium audio hardware and subscription streaming, Apple is perfectly positioned to turn this massive market overlap into music to its investors’ ears.

Update 11/2/2026 3:00 PM ET: As it turns out, the ultimate parent company and holder of all Tachyum intellectual property is Cayman Islands-based Tachyum Ltd., which controls U.S.-based Tachyum Inc., which in turn controls Slovakia-based Tachyum s.r.o. that is responsible for the lion’s share of Tachyum’s development of the Prodigy universal processor. This means that while Tachyum Inc. and Tachyum s.r.o. can be declared insolvent and liquidated, Tachyum Ltd. can continue operations, establish new entities and continue developing Prodigy.However, the Cayman Islands company holding Prodigy-related patents is itself the target of liquidation proceedings. Therefore, the Slovak subsidiary’s bankruptcy cannot necessarily protect Prodigy’s intellectual property from creditors. If Tachyum Ltd. is liquidated, the control over the Prodigy patents could pass to court-appointed liquidators, who could sell them to repay creditors. While the current Tachyum management could buy Prodigy’s patents back cheaply, they would have to compete with other interested buyers and satisfy the applicable sale requirements. In any case, this could be the end of the road for Tachyum.

Tachyum, the company behind the overpromised and overhyped universal Prodigy processor, has filed for bankruptcy in Bratislava, Slovakia, reports Forbes (as observed by @System360Cheese). The filing follows a court order initiating bankruptcy proceeding after the company repeatedly missed its development and production milestones — but there are still theoretical chances that development of the processor will continue.

Despite eight years of development and numerous promises, Tachyum has yet to demonstrate working Prodigy silicon. Tachyum introduced Prodigy in 2018, targeting a 2019 tape-out and 2020 commercial availability. But the company repeatedly postponed the processor's launch, first to 2021, then to 2022, 2023, 2024, and eventually 2025.

Meanwhile, Prodigy's specifications changed considerably along the line: The original 64-core design evolved into a 128-core processor manufactured on a 5nm-class process technology, then a 192-core chip with 16 DDR5 memory channels. In late 2025, Tachyum announced yet another radical redesign: a chiplet-based architecture with 1,024 cores, 24 DDR5 memory channels, and TDP of 1,600W manufactured using TSMC's 2nm-class node. The redesign would require substantial additional development work and would have delayed commercial availability until 2030 or beyond.

According to court documents cited by Forbes, Tachyum Slovakia itself filed for bankruptcy on October 22, 2026, without waiting for a petition from creditors seeking to recover unpaid debts. The Bratislava III Municipal Court subsequently initiated bankruptcy proceedings after determining that the company's petition met the legal requirements. Under Slovak law, a company that voluntarily files for bankruptcy is presumed insolvent, according to Forbes, so technically Tachyum Slovakia is bankrupt.

If the court formally declares Tachyum bankrupt, a court-appointed trustee will take control of the company's assets, which could then be sold to repay creditors. We do not know at this point what these assets are, but theoretically they may include intellectual property related to its Prodigy processor, patents, and other technologies in addition to hardware used for development. Unless Tachyum secures additional financing or finds a buyer that can fund further development, work on Prodigy could effectively end.

Bankruptcy proceedings against Tachyum's Slovak entity do not necessarily mean that its affiliated companies elsewhere will also cease operations. Furthermore, the company's IP could survive under new ownership (if the company finds a buyer, or transfers IP ownership to another entity), which could theoretically let Prodigy development to continue. Nevertheless, the bankruptcy filing casts serious doubt on Tachyum's ability or intention to bring its long-delayed processor to market.

Theoretically, Tachyum's owners could potentially use bankruptcy proceedings to shed the company's debts, acquire its intellectual property through another legal entity, and resume Prodigy development. There are other options too.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Although most of Tachyum development activities are concentrated in Slovakia, Tachyum Slovakia is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based Tachyum Inc. according to Dennik N. If the American parent company owns the Prodigy IP, while the Slovak subsidiary employs engineers, conducts development, and accumulates debts, bankruptcy could enable the group to eliminate a substantial portion of those liabilities without losing its most valuable technological assets. In short, Tachyum's Slovak subsidiary could disappear along with much of its unpaid debt, while the American parent retains Prodigy IP and attempts to commercialize it somehow in the future. If the Slovak subsidiary owns the IP, the American parent could theoretically buy it from the bankruptcy estate and attempt to commercialize it eventually. Meanwhile, there is another complication: The American parent has reportedly faced pressure from its own creditors, some of whom have requested its liquidation, according to Dennik N. In this case, the destiny of the Prodigy IP is completely unclear.

For now, the future of Prodigy may depend on who actually owns Prodigy's intellectual property — Tachyum Inc. in the U.S. or Tachyum Slovakia — and whether the American subsidiary continues to exist or gets liquidated. The answer could determine whether this bankruptcy represents the end of Prodigy or a restructuring of the Tachyum group with the aim to continue development.

#10459. Stop climbing the wrong career mountain

In November 2015, I booked a suite in a midtown Manhattan hotel and spent the night pacing, rehearsing my presentation in an empty room. The next morning I would host the first breakfast workshop for my new wealth advisory firm. I had left a prominent position as a director of wealth management at Morgan Stanley to build a company based on a radically different idea of wealth.

My guests included a senior partner at a private equity firm managing more than $10 billion and the head of a major firm’s wealth management division. I was about to tell them, “You’re chasing the wrong prize.” I was worried: What if they laughed when I said words like “heartfelt” and “holistic”?

But I couldn’t help myself. For years I’d privately suspected I was climbing the wrong mountain, and I’d realized it wasn’t just me.

The Wrong Measures of Success

Working on Wall Street had become an object lesson in the drawbacks of ceaseless competition. I loved my job, but there was no denying that it was an industry built on the glorification of money, privilege, and power. In finance, relentless pursuit—of richer clients, bigger accounts, and fatter fees—was a given, whatever the personal cost.

It isn’t just finance. Modern life trains all of us to pour most of our energy into our careers, even when the payoff is anxiety, exhaustion, and a nagging sense that something essential is missing. We’re overinvested in a faulty vision of success that pushes us constantly toward achievement, often at the cost of our health, our emotional well-being, and our relationships.

Despite our best intentions, so many of us are climbing the wrong mountain.

Here’s the problem. When net worth, title, and achievement are your only gauges, they can only tell you how high you’ve climbed. They can’t tell you whether you’re on the right mountain—the one that’s right for you.

I’ve learned the hard way that there is no way to win this game. There is only constant striving. The only way to “win” is to change the game completely, which means redefining wealth.

A New Definition of Wealth

Merriam-Webster defines wealth as an abundance of material possessions or resources. But the word comes from the Old English weal, meaning welfare or well-being. Somewhere along the way, we traded well-being for accumulation, and we’ve paid the price.

What I hadn’t yet realized was that I was yearning for a broader, more inclusive definition of success and wealth. My philosophical and spiritual studies pointed me to the fact that there was so much more than the limited definition I’d unconsciously adopted. Everything clicked when I read the work of Ken Wilber, whose Integral theory reveals how seemingly unrelated parts of life fit together as one vital whole. For the first time, I could see that well-being isn’t something you chase at the expense of everything else.

A Better Map for the Right Mountain

Guided by that vision, I had created a simple map that identifies four primary sources of wealth that comprise a truly rich life, which I now call The Four Quadrants of True Wealth, including:

  • Mind-Body Awareness: emotions, spirituality, and inner exploration
  • Work & Wealth Abundance: professional success and building net worth
  • Heartfelt Community Connection: community and rich relationships
  • Lifelong Learning: insight into how the world works

Most of us are well versed in one or two of these and neglect the others. That imbalance leaves us with a gnawing, ill-defined sense that something is out of whack.

After breakfast that morning at the hotel, I ushered the group into a room with a circle of chairs for the remainder of the workshop. Then I asked everyone to imagine the room divided into the four quadrants and posed a question all of us would do well to ask: Of these four dimensions of your life, where do you spend most of your time?

I invited them to walk to that corner. All eight crowded into the same one. We laughed at the sight of everyone sardined together in Work & Wealth Abundance.

Then I asked a second question: If you didn’t have to worry about money or resources, where would you like to spend your time?

The pack scattered across all four quadrants. An intellectual, Ivy League-educated investment banker headed for Lifelong Learning. Another guest, a lovable man with loads of friends and a wonderful family, walked to Mind-Body Awareness and admitted, “Honestly, Matt, I have no idea what my feelings even are!”

I would have gone to Heartfelt Community Connection. Work and inner life were strengths by then, but I’d grown lonely pursuing both.

By exploring different forms of wealth that morning, each of us found areas where we felt surprisingly poor. The room’s energy shifted, with more openness, warmth, and trust than we were used to in our business lives. Jennie Liang, a marketing consultant who was there, recalls: “Everyone arrived in suits looking very professional, but vulnerability took over. Heading back to work, it felt like putting my armor back on.”

The Four Quadrants of True Wealth: Try It Yourself

The Four Quadrants of True Wealth is a self-diagnostic tool that lets you easily see how to create balance in your life. Ask yourself the same two questions:

  • Where do I spend most of my time?
  • If money weren’t a worry, where would I want to spend it?

Once you see what’s missing, you can’t unsee it. Small changes in one or two neglected quadrants can bring disproportionately large benefits. This is not about juggling more. It’s about widening your perspective so you can make more skillful choices and move from constantly striving for achievement to finding fulfillment. That’s how you find the right mountain: not the one you were told to climb, but the one that’s truly yours.

#10457. Bad memory: Some chip stocks are tumbling despite the broader post-election rally for tech. Here’s why

Tuesday’s blue tsunami didn’t just boost the Democrats’ fortunes. The 2026 midterm results also fueled a surge in the stock market, with all but a few Big Tech stocks seeing notable gains. 

But memory chip stocks told a different story. Shares in the four major memory chipmakers all saw steep declines. And those declines are continuing today. Here’s what you need to know.

The midterm results boosted the markets

Yesterday was a stellar day for many of the biggest-name companies traded on the markets. And a stellar day for the markets in general. As CNN noted, the Dow had its best post-midterm-election day in 44 years, with a jump of about 3%, or 1,569 points.

The S&P 500 jumped 1.58%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 1.44%.

When it comes to individual stocks, Big Tech (mostly) had a great day.

Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT) ended the day up 6.6%, Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL) rose 5.3%, Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN) jumped 6.1%, Netflix, Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) rose 4.6%, Alphabet Inc. (Nasdaq: GOOG) was up 3.2%, and Meta Platforms, Inc. (Nasdaq: META) was up 1.4%. 

As of the time of this writing, all those companies are continuing to see gains in premarket trading this morning, too.

The main reason for the stock market’s big day yesterday was the certainty brought by the Democrats’ decisive victory. There is no question about which party will hold the levers of power in Congress when its members are sworn in in January. Investors hate uncertainty, and the Democrats’ historic win all but eliminated it.

Memory chipmakers left out of the rally

Despite the broader gains, yesterday was not a good day for one type of company in particular: memory chipmakers.

Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) saw its stock sink 7%, SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK) fell 7.9%, Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC) dropped 6.7%, and Seagate Technology Holdings plc(Nasdaq: STX) fell a staggering 8.1%.

And yes, the election results were likely to blame for those drops, too.

Unfortunately for investors in memory chip companies, yesterday’s massive drop in memory chip shares doesn’t seem to be a one-off. In premarket trading this morning, memory stocks are once again getting hammered, as of the time of this writing.

  • Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down nearly 4%
  • SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 5.3%
  • Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC): down 4.7%
  • Seagate Technology Holdings plc (Nasdaq: STX): down 4.5%

Why are memory chip stocks falling?

The main worry investors seem to have is that the midterm election results weren’t just a referendum on the Republican Party, which currently controls Congress, and the Trump administration. 

Yes, Americans punished both for rising prices and an unpopular war, but another issue was also top of mind in many state and local elections: data centers.

Many of the Democrats who won those elections ran on an anti-AI and anti-data center stance, promising either moratoriums or restrictions on the building of the unpopular server farms that are popping up across the country.

And now many of those Democrats hold the levers of power not just in Washington, but also locally, where the data centers are being built.

Any reining in of the data center expansion is bad news for memory chipmakers.

Data centers need servers to run AI, and those servers need massive amounts of RAM. If data center buildouts slow, the demand for RAM shrinks at a commensurate rate. And that’s bad for memory chipmakers’ bottom lines.

Voters are unified in their opposition to data centers

There are few issues that both the left and right can agree on, but one of them is their dislike for data centers.

As noted by Reuters, an NBC and SSRS exit poll revealed that around 76% of voters opposed new data centers being built where they lived.

Those voters just sent a massive blue wave to Washington, and that doesn’t bode well for an increased data center buildout.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk quipped, alluding to the opposition that terrestrial data centers now face.

Other billionaires were more foreboding.

As noted by CNBC, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya warned that “the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers.”

Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned that slowing AI development could put America’s tech advantage in danger, declaring, “Practically speaking, we can’t slow down.”

Yet given the sinking stock prices of memory chip and storage makers, a slowdown is exactly what investors seem to think is coming.

#10456. Reddit will soon be a ‘logged-in-only’ website, forcing you to have an account

Reddit is shifting to a “logged-in-only experience,” the company confirmed during its latest earnings call.

While the timeline is vague at this point, Reddit has confirmed that it will be locking down the site for users without an account, also impacting usage in private browsing modes. CEO Steve Huffman explains in a shareholder letter and a post on Reddit that the website will becoming a “logged-in-only experience.”

Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.

In Q4 we’ll begin fully testing this in select markets outside the U.S. The results of those tests will inform an optimized version of logged-in-only Reddit globally.

The change also comes as Reddit says that search referral traffic was “down meaningfully” in Q3 2026, mainly in regards to logged-out traffic. “Down meaningfully” was later detailed to mean that traffic “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week.”

"It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data" What he means is they want to prevent access to Reddit's data, unless they get paid for it. What has always annoyed me about Reddit is that they think it is their data. Almost everything on the site is generated by users, it's their data, not Reddit's.

As for private browsing, Huffman says that Reddit has “rebuilt and [is] re-releasing incognito mode in our app.”

Details on what will and will not be available to logged-out users are unclear at this time, though Huffman says that “the front page being available logged-out is useful and important,” adding that “visitors arriving from search or other external sources to see the content that’s being linked to.” He further implies that AI scraping is certainly a major part of this decision, saying that “the vast majority of unauthorized access to Reddit (basically the scraping and stealing of Reddit’s data) happens through our logged-out experiences.”

This comes shortly after Reddit rolled out a new personalized “For You” homepage.

OpenAI plans community agreements and infrastructure commitments as it prepares to rebrand data centers amid growing public opposition

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI is reportedly preparing a major public relations campaign to influence how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as “AI Compute Campuses,” Axios reports. The initiative comes ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and forms a broader effort to influence the debate around AI before the 2028 presidential race. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, noted that the midterms would be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” He expects AI to be a major issue for presidential candidates as the technology raises concerns over its impact on jobs, the economy, and the environment.

The proposed terminology change by OpenAI has been ongoing since August as the company focuses on promoting safeguards for the powerful technology, which Lehane described as “speed limits.” The proposed AI compute campuses is particularly interesting as it comes as opposition to large data centers accelerates across the U.S. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. OpenAI hopes to address these concerns through community agreements and a different way of presenting the infrastructure. “Compute campuses better describe the role of the infrastructure we are rebuilding for AI," a company spokesperson separately stated. He added that these projects represent long term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs.

The latest proposal follows similar efforts by other technology companies to improve their relationship with communities hosting their infrastructure. In January, Microsoft announced a community-first approach, promising to cover electricity cost increases associated with its data centers, and invest in local infrastructure and jobs. However, while changing the name may be easier, changing public opinion may bring some headaches. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed are opposed to having a new data center built in their community. Another report in August detailed how negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently take place behind non-disclosure agreements, leaving residents without access to important project information.

The resistance has also affected actual construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have already moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle’s $16 billion Stargate project went ahead with their project in Sanile township despite local opposition. Meanwhile, Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback.

OpenAI is not alone in trying to reshape the language surrounding AI. President Donald Trump has previously pushed for terminology change, directing Federal agencies and urging AI companies to replace artificial intelligence with ‘super intelligence.’ Trump announced the change in late September arguing that the word "artificial" made the technology sound "fake." His administration subsequently instructed state department employees to use super intelligence or SI in official directives, websites, reports and policy documents.

Some technology executives have also embraced the terminology. Nvidia CEO Huang has previously referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories" while Elon musk announced plans to rename his AI company SpaceXAI to SpacexSI last month. Meta, meanwhile, established Meta superintelligence labs in 2025, and Microsoft has also assembled a team focused on developing superintelligence. OpenAI’s proposed terminology will now face a more difficult test than simply finding a name as communities will still want answers about the raised issues. Lehane, however, acknowledged that public scrutiny is part of the process saying, “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.”

#10451. What is Trump’s next move on his unpopular Iran war, now that the midterms are over?

As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.

For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.

In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.

“It’s largely true because it drove gasoline up a little bit,” Trump said. Still, he doubled down on his decision to launch the conflict despite its big political cost. “At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d do it again,” he said.

The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.

Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.

Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated

While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting it out.

The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.

The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.

The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.

“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”

Trump has at least a few options, analysts say

Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.

Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.

Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran’s nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.

Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.

But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.

Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next

Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.

Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.

Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he’d have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.

A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.

Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP’s candidates for the big loss.

“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”

Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump’s decision once he made it.

Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue

Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets on Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.

“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”

About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.

Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.

Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.

Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”

Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.

But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he’d approach Iran exactly as he has.

“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different,” the president said.

AP writers Collin Binkley, Hannah Fingerhut, and Kathleen Foody contributed reporting.

—Aamer Madhani, Linley Sanders, Samy Magdy and Matthew Lee, Associated Press

Pin is built for recruiting teams that want sourcing, outreach and interview scheduling in one product, and it is trusted by 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users. SHRM found AI use in HR tasks reached 43% of organizations in 2025, up from 26% in 2024. Some comparisons call Pin a solo-recruiter tool. This one checks Pin and Juicebox against their current public pages.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that automates the top of the funnel, from sourcing and outreach to interview scheduling, for solo recruiters, agencies and in-house teams. Juicebox (PeopleGPT) is an AI sourcing platform that pairs natural-language candidate search with outreach sequences, ATS and CRM integrations, and add-on AI agents. For a longer feature-by-feature breakdown, see Pin's Pin vs Juicebox comparison.

No. Pin has a one-seat Solo plan at $99 a month on annual billing, and solo recruiters and small agencies use it. But Pin's team features and pricing are built for multiple users:

Juicebox does team work too. According to its pricing page (October 2026), Growth lets you invite up to five teammates to collaborate on searches, shortlists and outreach, and Business adds hiring-manager seats, usage analytics and ATS or CRM integration. Pin's team pages describe hiring managers, sourcers and closers sharing one view of the req.

Pin says it searches 850M+ profiles across multiple sources, including North America and Europe, aggregated from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. You can search in plain language, paste a job description, upload ideal résumés or import a role from your ATS. Each ranked candidate gets a fit score and an AI-written reason, and the model learns from accept and reject feedback across the team.

Juicebox offers natural-language search over a stated 800 million profiles from "30+" sources, and its AI Spotlight also explains why a candidate matches. It adds three data features worth knowing about:

Pin lists Talent Insights on Professional and Business too. Profile counts say little about quality, so run the same roles in both. If you are also pricing LinkedIn's tool, see LinkedIn Recruiter alternatives.

Pin runs multi-channel sequences across email, LinkedIn and SMS: automated email steps plus AI-drafted LinkedIn and SMS tasks in the same sequence, which the recruiter sends. Pin reports those sequences deliver 5x better response rates than industry averages, benchmarked against LinkedIn's published 10-25% InMail reply rates. Pin drafts each message from the candidate's own profile signals and calibrates to your writing voice. Sequences adapt per candidate, any reply pauses the sequence, and every channel stays in one thread. The Free plan is email-only, multi-channel sequences start on Solo, and Professional includes five mailboxes per user.

Juicebox's outreach page (October 2026) describes "email, calls, and social touches in one sequence," automatic stop on reply and analytics by step and channel. Growth includes three mailboxes per seat, Business six. Its agents page describes agent outreach as email only.

No. Pin's AI recruiting agent has two modes. In Assist, you approve each step. In Autopilot, the agent sources, screens and ranks, drafts outreach, sends the email steps, follows up on silence, schedules interviews and updates the ATS. LinkedIn and SMS steps queue as tasks with AI-drafted messages that the recruiter sends. Pin assists recruiters and never replaces them: closing and offers stay human. Human-in-the-loop guardrails apply, and every action appears in a feed. Pin saves recruiters 12 hours per week on sourcing and outreach combined, according to Pin's 2026 user survey across 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users.

It is also steerable. Pin asks clarifying questions about the brief, such as "Is remote considered?", and you refine in plain language. Josh Volinsky, Co-Founder of Synergy Search, says: "Pin makes sourcing candidates so natural and I love how you can just talk to it like it's a recruiter on your team and it goes hunting."

Pin's MCP server lets you work from Claude Desktop, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex: start searches, review candidates, tune the search in plain language and keep per-job memory. Pin says "You still approve every accept, reject, and outreach." It is free on every paid plan.

Juicebox's agents are steerable too. According to its agents page (October 2026), you recalibrate by chatting with the agent, with autonomy from fully hands-off to manual checkpoints at shortlist or sequencing. Its MCP server, launched in August 2026, launches agents and pulls usage and reply-rate reports. The agents page does not describe interview scheduling, and each agent is a separate $199 monthly add-on.

So the differences are scope and price, not steerability. For the wider field, see best AI recruiting agents.

Five recruiters need Pin Professional or Juicebox Growth, because Juicebox Starter is one seat. Prices are list prices published October 14, 2026.

Credits are metered differently. Pin charges 1 credit per personal email, work email or phone number. According to Juicebox's credits documentation (October 2026), an email is 1 credit and a phone number is 3. Revealing email plus phone costs 2 credits on Pin and 4 on Juicebox, so the included allowance covers about 2,500 full contacts a month on Pin and 1,875 on Juicebox.

Past five recruiters, Juicebox requires Business, which is custom-priced and annual only.

Price history. According to Juicebox's archived pricing pages, Growth cost $99 per seat per month billed annually in April 2024, with up to 10 seats and 250 contact credits. Today it is $179, up to 5 seats and 1,500 credits. In March 2026 alone, the monthly Growth price rose from $179 to $199 per seat, and agents moved from $300 for two to $199 each. Confirm current prices on Pin's pricing page and on Juicebox's own pricing page. For what reviewers say about the cost, see Juicebox AI reviews 2026.

Both list SOC 2 Type II. Pin's trust center covers SOC 2 Type 2 (third-party audited), encryption at rest and in transit, and GDPR and CCPA readiness. Juicebox lists SSO and role-based access control.

On AI fairness, both vendors now have third-party work behind them. Pin uses third-party fairness audits and feeds no names, gender or protected characteristics to the AI, with checkpoints at every step and regular team reviews of AI outputs. Its trust center lists a Pin Algorithmic Fairness Report (August 2026), available on request.

Juicebox posts its audit dashboard publicly, hosted by Warden AI, a third-party assurance provider. It showed monthly audits of Juicebox's Autopilot candidate-ranking feature, the latest dated August 6, 2026, with reports for NYC Local Law 144, the EU AI Act, Colorado and California.

Whichever tool you choose, request the bias documentation. Gartner's 2025 survey of 2,918 job candidates found only 26% trust AI to evaluate them fairly. New York City's Local Law 144 requires a bias audit within a year of using an automated employment decision tool. Ask counsel whether a sourcing tool counts.

For recruiting teams and agencies that want one product from sourcing through scheduling, Pin covers that whole flow.

Choose Pin if: - You want sourcing, outreach, scheduling and ATS updates in one product, with a shared inbox. - You have or expect more than five recruiters, or run an agency needing a multi-client CRM. - You want agents included in the seat price, plus a free start.

Juicebox is good for: - Teams that need hiring-manager seats to review shortlists, on its custom-priced Business plan. - Teams that value compensation estimates (Growth and up) or warm-intro network sourcing (Business only).

When Pin is not the right fit: teams that only need high-volume inbound applicant screening.

#10449. IQOO’s new mid-range phone puts last year’s flagships to shame

The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget.

Companies like IQOO often surprise with specs that feel like they shouldn’t belong on relatively inexpensive phones, and the IQOO Neo 12 fits right in with that. The star of the show is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, the same one in the $1300 Galaxy S26 Ultra. That’s made even better thanks to a custom 59-blade active cooling fan and a “3D Ice Dome” vapor chamber inside.

On the front is a generous 6.83-inch 185Hz AMOLED panel with 2K resolution, a 2,200-nit peak brightness rate, and both DC dimming and 2,160Hz PWM dimming for eye comfort. Unsurprisingly, for a gaming-centric phone, it’s also got a custom display chip for IQOO 16-level touch responsiveness and a “super-sensitive gyro” for epic gyro aiming in games.

Despite having an active fan, this one features an IP69 rating, so it can be abused in all sorts of ways without seeing water or dust damage. A 9,000mAh battery is inside with support for 100W wired charging, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, IR sensor, and stereo speakers round out the build.

The IQOO Neo 12 packs a 50MP Sony IMX921 main camera sensor alongside an 8MP ultra-wide camera in the stylish raised camera island on the back, plus a 16MP selfie up front. Phone colorway options include Contender, Frost Blade Blue, and Shadow Black. This one is making its initial debut in China for:

Not too shabby, given the specs. Chinese users can buy it from Vivo right now. A global release date has not yet been announced.

Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.

Update: Amazon just closed my account.Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist. Be careful!November 1, 2026

Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.

The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.

Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”

He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”

Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.

With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.

Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.

Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.

Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

#10445. Many of UGREEN’s best NAS units are 10-15% off right now

A NAS is way easier and cheaper than you think, thanks to UGREEN NAS units and a great little Amazon sale.

For years, I went about my day juggling several different external hard drives to offload the obscene number of photos and videos I capture for my job. I thought NAS — that’s Network Attached Storage — were simply too complicated for home use until I used a UGREEN NAS. It completely changed my perspective on the tech, and I guarantee it’ll do the same for you.

UGREEN makes a bunch of different NAS units, all of which are impressively highly rated (only one of 20 on Amazon is rated less than 4.5/5 stars), and around half a dozen of those are between 10-15% off right now:

Don’t get confused by the names. The DH series is meant primarily for home use, while the DX series is meant for either home offices or small offices. The main difference is in storage capacity and capability.

The home-use DH series works as a great way to cut down on all those annoying cloud storage subscription costs and ensure that your data stays in your home instead of some data center. If you’ve got a sizable movie collection, you can also digitize it and turn it into a streaming media server. It’s super cool and a great addition to simply storing all those files that no longer fit on your computer.

Yeah, it’s a lot, and it feels like there’s something new every week. If you just want one for your home, choose the DH2300 if you just need an easy way to store extra files. Otherwise, upgrade to the DXP2800 if the idea of running containerized apps and personal servers sounds like your jam.

Just 128MB of RAM is enough to boot Windows 11.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NTDEV, the popular developer behind the Tiny11 project, has once again pushed the limits of just how little hardware is required to run Windows 11. In a video shared on YouTube, the developer claims to have successfully booted the latest Windows 11 26H2 on a system with just 128MB of RAM. Despite severe memory constraints, the heavily stripped-down installation manages to load the Desktop and File Explorer, access the Start menu, and even run the classic Notepad app.

While it is an impressive achievement, the developer acknowledges that the system is "painfully slow," making this more of a technical experiment than a practical way to run Windows 11 on older hardware. According to Microsoft’s official requirements, Windows 11 requires at least 4GB of RAM, meaning NTDEV's latest experiment uses just 3.125% of the recommended minimum. The developer has not shared a detailed breakdown of every component removed or disabled to achieve the result, but the project builds on years of experimentation with stripped-down Windows installations.

This is not NTDEV's first attempt at pushing Windows 11 beyond its usual hardware limitations. Back in 2023, the developer managed to get the operating system running with only 176MB of RAM by extensively trimming its system components, drivers, and background services. That experiment relied on an IDE storage interface to reduce the number of drivers required, and sacrificed the standard Windows desktop environment.

Last month, the developer showcased another interesting experiment that squeezed an entire Windows 11 installation into a CD-ROM-sized ISO file. The experimental build created using the developer's upcoming Pico11 tool weighs in at 699,811,840 bytes and retains a functional Windows desktop. The stripped-down version of Windows 11 successfully boots into the desktop environment and runs basic applications such as Calculator, Settings, Notepad, and Paint. The test was conducted on a virtual machine with 4GB of allocated RAM, with the operating system using around 883MB.

Such experiments are a great way to showcase just how much of Windows can be stripped away while still retaining some of its core functionality. At the end of the day, they are primarily technical demonstrations with the intention of exploring the limits of Microsoft's operating system rather than providing practical alternatives to a standard Windows installation. Stripping away essential components, drivers, and background services comes with significant trade-offs, including reduced functionality, compatibility issues, and severely degraded performance.
